entries: Inherited from Middle High German anesetzen, from Old High German anasezzen. Analyzable as an- + setzen. Compare English onset.
senses: to set, to place, ready (an implement or tool in the required position for its usage, implying an intent to start using it, e.g. a chisel on stone, a pen on paper, a bottle on the lips)
to schedule, to set (a meeting, a procedure, an election)
to prepare (a concoction or mixture, such as to start a process that results in the intended product, e.g. fermentation or acquiring a certain aroma)
to develop, to start forming (seeds, rust, a patina, etc.)
to set someone on something or someone, to set someone to some task (e.g. tracking dogs on a person, detectives or lawyers on a case, workers on a problem)
to begin, to attempt (an act, especially movement, either being interrupted or not yet having had the chance to fully perform it)

entries: Inherited from Middle High German genæme, from Old High German gināmi, from Proto-West Germanic *ganāmī, a prefixed form of a verbal adjective from the root of nehmen (“to take”).
senses: politically convenient (preferred specifically because it lines up with one's political agenda, e.g. of results or foreign leaders)
divide, dividing line, parting line, separating line
